author: Omar Kalinge-Nnyago
title: Uganda: The Entrenchment of a Hereditary Military Oligarchy
content:
Uganda is approaching one of the most precarious political transitions in its post-independence history. The likely trajectory is not democratic consolidation but the slow institutionalization of a hereditary military oligarchy. Four developments are driving this shift: President Yoweri Museveni’s advanced age; the elevation of his son, Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, to Chief of Defence Forces (CDF); the operationalization of the Patriotic League of Uganda (PLU) as a parallel mobilization vehicle; and the legal entrenchment of military authority over civilian institutions. Taken together, these amount to what might be called a “slow-motion coup” already under way.


The most probable outcome is best described as contested dynastic authoritarianism, a system in which elections continue to serve as instruments of international legitimacy, while substantive power is contested within the first family and the military elite rather than at the ballot box. The formal opposition faces structural decapitation through repression and co-optation. Yet two under-examined institutions – the Anglican and Catholic Churches, and segments of Uganda’s Muslim community – offer potential, if imperfect, nonviolent pathways for mediation or resistance over the coming decade, complicated by the risk of Muslim youth radicalization.


A conventional, extra-constitutional military coup remains possible even as the regime works to secure de facto military dominance through promotions, strategic retirements of senior officers, legislative amendment, and patronage. The PLU’s grassroots strategy is designed to insulate the succession from exactly this risk, cultivating broad loyalty and framing dynastic continuity as patriotic inevitability rather than rupture. The principal danger to the plan, accordingly, lies less in popular revolt than in intra-elite fracture or palace intrigue should the succession falter.


Anatomy of a slow-motion coup


The regime has moved beyond personalist autocracy toward a durable, self-perpetuating system built on four pillars: fusion of military command with the first family, political mobilization through the PLU, subordination of parliament, and kleptocratic control of the state’s resources.


Uganda’s slide toward dynastic rule no longer needs to be projected; it can be observed directly. In 2024, Museveni handed his son the office of Chief of Defence Forces, together with an unusual personal grant of authority to promote senior officers – a clear departure from the constitutional design of a professional military answerable to civilian rather than familial command. Muhoozi has used this platform expansively, maintaining an active, often combative social media presence, intervening openly in partisan disputes, and, in June 2026, ordering troops to shut down Nation Media Group’s operations after critical coverage of his conduct. He has also directly ordered the arrest of opposition lawyer Erias Lukwago and the deportation of Kenyan lawyer Martha Karua, both members of Dr Kizza Besigye’s defence team – a signal that the regime now treats defence counsel, and not only defendants, as targets. In his national address of 4 July 2026, President Museveni appeared to defend his son’s actions, placing blame on Besigye for allegedly delaying court proceedings.


The institutional scaffolding around Muhoozi has matured alongside his personal profile. The Patriotic League of Uganda, rebranded in 2024 from an informal network of birthday rallies and fan clubs known as the “Muhoozi Project”, now runs village-level structures, community clean-up campaigns, and youth roadshows, and openly courts the same rural base the National Resistance Movement (NRM) has cultivated for four decades. It functions less as a political party than as an insurance policy: it absorbs potential rivals into patronage, builds a loyalty network running parallel to the NRM’s own, and softens the ground for a hereditary handover by presenting it as continuity rather than rupture. Leadership changes, such as the appointment of Hon. Fadil Twaha as Secretary General, signal a deliberate effort to deepen outreach among Muslim communities that feel marginalized in the League’s rise.


The 12

th

 Parliament offered an early demonstration of the PLU’s reach. The League withdrew its earlier backing for then Speaker Anita Among and her deputy, Thomas Tayebwa, clearing the way for Jacob Oboth-Oboth’s election as Speaker – a small but telling exercise of veto power …

author: ROAPE
title: Bought, held, and sworn
content:
Somalia’s parliamentary election is not one election. It is 275 simultaneous, separate auctions. Each of Somalia’s 275 House of the People seats belongs to a specific sub-clan. Each is contested by a separate and distinct pool of delegates — assembled only for that seat, voting only on that seat, with no overlap with any other. What looks from outside like a single national election is, on the ground, 275 parallel closed markets operating at the same time — each with its own elder-broker, its own candidate payments, its own hotel rooms full of men who have been paid, sequestered, and made to swear on the Quran before they are allowed to vote. This is not electoral dysfunction. It is the operational logic of a system designed to convert clan identity and foreign financing into a self-reproducing governing class — one that controls parliament, elects the president, and uses both to block accountability for those who commit abuses in its service.


This investigation draws on primary source interviews with more than a dozen electoral delegates, parliamentary candidates, and traditional clan elders who participated directly in Somalia’s 2016–2017 and 2021–2022 parliamentary election cycles. It is corroborated by field research conducted by

Marqaati

 — Somalia’s leading independent accountability organisation — across five federal states, and by an academic study of Somalia’s electoral corruption published in the International Journal of Multicultural and Multireligious Understanding (

Bincof, 2023

). The companion piece to this investigation, “The Debt That Governs,” documents what happens next: how the parliament assembled through this process feeds directly into the presidential election — and how the president who emerges repays his debt through Somalia’s ports, procurement budget, and foreign policy.


The hotel room


The invitation arrives as a courtesy. A candidate’s representative calls to say there will be a dinner — a chance to meet the person seeking the parliamentary seat, to hear their plans, to share a meal. The delegate, one of those chosen by his sub-clan elder to cast a vote for their specific seat, accepts. It seems reasonable. It seems normal. It is neither.


After the dinner — plates of rice and camel meat, sweet tea, pleasantries — the delegates are not taken home. They are taken to a hotel. Or a large private residence. Somewhere with rooms, with guards, with doors that are not locked but might as well be. They are fed again the next morning. And the morning after that. Their phones are watched. Their movements are noted. And at some point, over tea or in a quiet room, they are asked to place their right hand on the Quran and swear that their vote, when election day finally comes, belongs to the candidate who is feeding them.


“They take you to a hotel. They feed you. They watch you. And then they make you swear on the Quran. After that, you are not a delegate anymore. You are a captive.” — A former delegate, speaking on condition of anonymity


This is not an isolated incident. The same sequence emerged with striking consistency across both the 2016–2017 and 2021–2022 election cycles: the invitation, the dinner, the hotel, the oath, the vote. And it is happening not once but 275 times simultaneously — one operation for each of Somalia’s 275 parliamentary seats, across every contested race in the country, at the same time.


How the system is built


On paper, Somalia’s indirect election system is a carefully constructed compromise. In a country with no functioning voter registration infrastructure and a political landscape organised primarily along clan lines, each of the 275 seats in the House of the People belongs to a specific sub-clan. The four major clans — Hawiye, Darod, Dir, and Digil and Mirifle — receive 61 seats each, and every smaller and minority clan is folded into a single combined share of 31 — a structure known simply as the “4.5” system: four equal shares for the big clans, half a share for everyone else. Each seat belongs to a precise lineage group within those larger blocs, and competition for it is always internal — always within the sub-clan, always intimate.


In the 2016–2017 cycle, each seat had 51 delegates, giving a total delegate universe of approximately 14,025 people across all 275 seats. By the 2021–2022 cycle, that pool had grown to 101 delegates per seat — approximately 27,775 people in total. Each delegate pool is its own closed market: its own elder, its own …

author: Suliman Baldo
title: Why Sanctions Are Not Stifling Sudan’s War Economy and What We Can Do About It
content:
Since the outbreak of the brutal civil war in Sudan in April 2023, the US, British, and Canadian governments, along with the European Union and United Nations, have imposed targeted sanctions on some 32 individuals and 20 companies tied to the bloodshed to restrict their access to assets, international finance, and travel. Three and a half years into the fighting, more than two-thirds of Sudan’s population requires humanitarian aid and almost 14 million people have been forcibly displaced, and the need for effective policy responses has never been more urgent.


These sanctions have had some impact. For example, China, citing international sanctions, refused to authorise the sale of its air defence systems by Pakistan to Sudan in August 2025. Turkey refused a deal to sell drones to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) because the group was unable to provide an end-user licence. Succumbing to pressure, the UAE has

distanced itself

 from some shell companies previously operating as covers for the RSF from its soil.


More often, however, it has been easy for sanctioned entities to obfuscate and manoeuvre around sanctions, sometimes in the very capitals that have issued them.


Earlier this year, a business forum convened in London to mobilise capital to rebuild Sudan’s economy showed how those profiting from the conflict continue to evade sanctions. One of the event’s sponsors, the Export Development Group (EDG), presented itself as a leading player in Sudan’s future reconstruction.


A

new report

 by the Sudan Transparency and Policy Tracker (SPTP) argues that the company is, in fact, a subsidiary of the Defense Industries Systems (DIS), the military conglomerate that operates a web of businesses that finance the Sudan Armed Forces’ (SAF) war machine, which the UK government designated in June 2023. Operating in London and on its website, it obfuscates that connection, scrubbing any reference to its affiliation to its parent company from its website, with the imputed goal of distancing itself from the sanctions. At the same time, it continues to reference it in

social media posts

 intended for domestic audiences.


The Exports Development Group presents a different image in content for domestic audiences compared to its international profile.


Research published

 by STPT has identified the primary challenge in employing sanctions effectively. The designations issued to date have been drawn narrowly and enforced loosely, targeting specific individuals and companies, with targets adapting faster than the governments that target them.


A prime case is that of Zadna International, a DIS subsidiary sanctioned by the UK, US, and EU between June 2023 and January 2024. Despite this, the report argues that the company has become the primary beneficiary of massive contracts across areas controlled by the Sudanese Army and a conduit for war profiteering. In December 2025, the company was awarded an approximately $7 million contract to resurface a 12-mile road in Gezira state, a cost ten times higher than an estimate for the same work in a 2022 agreement, according to the STPT report.


In the same month, White Nile state reportedly named Zadna as the primary partner for all of its 2026 development projects. The company’s director described the strategy as ‘financial engineering,’ shifting its externally-sanctioned operations domestically.  Such ‘financial engineering’ involves structuring joint-venture trade partnerships in friendly countries—such as Egypt—and using commodity swaps to bypass international currency transactions, a mechanism detailed in a recent

STPT report

 and investigated by

The New Arab

.


Red Rock Mining Company, another DIS affiliate company sanctioned by the UK and EU, highlighted its operations in Tanzania, Ethiopia, the UAE, and the Netherlands, an EU member state,

on LinkedIn

 in November 2025.


LinkedIn post by Red Rock Mining.


Merghani Idriss, the head of DIS, is still alleged to lead major weapons procurements for the army, despite being sanctioned by Canada, the US, and the EU, reportedly leading a delegation to Pakistan to

sign

 a $230 million arms package, widely reported to have been

financed by Saudi Arabia

.


The DIS, two years into the conflict,

showcased

 its domestically manufactured drones and precision weapons at a Turkish defence fair.


Similarly, SAF’s main rival, the RSF, have employed similar tactics and adapted to sanction regimes. One of its primary vehicles …

author: Babatunde Opeyemi Salami
title: What Nollywood owes the ancestors
content:
In June 2025, in Lagos, I sat down with custodians of Yoruba masquerading traditions, and I asked each of them a version of the same question: “What do you think about masquerades appearing in Nigerian films?” Each time, the answer was a flat no.

I grew up in Lagos and have spent years studying Yoruba masquerading traditions, particularly

Eyo

 and

Igunnuko

. With support from the Ebrahim Hussein Fellowship and the Aliko Songolo Award, I conducted formal interviews at the Bajulaye and Alagbeji palaces and at the Igunnuko shrines in Epetedo and Alaguntan to understand where this resistance comes from. More importantly, I sought to know what it means for Nollywood to keep returning to these figures despite the pushback.

Foundational cultural theorists of the 1930s and 1940s grappled with a similar question of what happens when a sacred or ritual object is copied, restaged, or transferred into a new medium. In 1944, Theodor Adorno and Max Horkheimer believed that mechanical reproduction drains ritual objects of their meaning, while Walter Benjamin had argued the opposite about a decade earlier. For Benjamin, reproduction could free art from ritual’s grip rather than hollow it out. The reality of this tension is a concept that my fieldwork explores.

To understand the resistance to masquerade remediation in film, you first have to understand what a masquerade is to its custodians. In Yoruba tradition, the

egungun

 is not a costume design. It’s what a family member becomes after death, made visible.

Ile

, the family compound and infrastructure of domestic life, is what produces a person worth remembering. A properly raised person becomes, after death and burial within that same compound, an ancestor (

alaale

 or

babanla

). The cloth used to bury them,

ago

 or

eku

, is equal to the same cloth a masquerade wears.

Therefore, a masquerader is not an actor playing an ancestor; the masquerade is treated as an ancestral presence, returned. These masquerades are called

ara orun

 (heaven dwellers), and their presence has two faces: the ancestral side is what is made public, danced and seen at a festival, while

orisa

 is the sacred essence beneath it, hidden and guarded. None of this starts on the day a masquerade appears. It starts with the

ile

, a life, a death, a burial, a cloth. Once you skip that, what is left on a screen is the shape of a masquerade without the systems that make one real.

Interestingly, motion has always been the story of Yoruba masquerades. Scholars trace the tradition from the Nupe to the Oyo, who developed traditions like Ololu, still performed in Ibadan today. From Oyo it moved south, reshaped by Ijebu, home to the

Agemo

 and

Eyo

 masquerades. Historical accounts credit two Ijebu brothers, Malaki and Ejilu, with carrying Eyo onward to Eko, old Lagos, where it grew into the festival celebrated today. Therefore, studying masquerade in Lagos already means studying something remediated many times over, long before a camera entered the picture.

Following this trajectory, screen media is the newer remediation, and it works differently. Abba Makama’s

The Lost Okoroshi

 (2019) turned a security guard into a purple ancestral spirit, putting a masquerade at the center of a very modern Lagos story.

Jagun Jagun

 (2023), the Netflix epic produced by and starring

Femi Adebayo

, leaned hard on Yoruba spiritual and masquerade imagery and became one of the biggest Yoruba-language releases in years.

Gangs of Lagos

 is another Nigerian film that significantly employs the image of a masquerade tradition. Masquerades also appear constantly in music videos, almost always as background texture, with no voice of their own.

The rare film attempts have drawn public criticism and lawsuits from masquerade societies and state authorities, as in the case of

Gangs of Lagos

. However, nothing comparable has happened to a music video. The traditional masquerade falls under the supervision of a secret cult called

awo

, which sets the pace and protects

orisa

, the sacred core of the tradition. A film crew doesn’t move at that pace, and it certainly doesn’t answer to that authority.

Furthermore, the filmmakers see it differently. In my interviews with them, both Adebayo and Makama were clear that they aren’t trying to reproduce a masquerade as it exists. They’re making something new, despite drawing on existing traditions. Makama has said plainly that he wants Nigerians, especially younger …

author: Mada Masr
title: Youth and sports in rural areas: Greater access or declining participation?
content:
Increased state investment in youth and sports facilities was Sports Minister Gohar Nabil’s boast on the first day of the

Egypt Forum 2026

, as part of the government’s tour of its own

achievements

.


During a session titled “Youth and sports: From creating opportunities to making an impact,” Nabil

pointed

to more than LE31 billion spent on youth and sports facilities, including 4,382 youth centers, 23 sports stadiums, 40,000 youth center leagues, 12 youth and sports cities and 4,566 football pitches. He did not specify over what period those billions were spent.


Against the minister’s showpiece figures, the session made no mention of data from the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics, which show a sharp drop in the number of matches played and sports teams registered at village youth centers between

2013

 and

2024

, even as the number of centers went up.


According to CAPMAS’s 2013 and 2024 annual bulletins, the number of matches played by sports teams at village youth centers fell by 85.5 percent over the decade.


During the same period, the number of sports teams dropped by 50.3 percent, even though the number of centers rose by 6.7 percent.


The decline in the number of matches also extended to city youth centers, though at a slower rate. Matches there fell by 50.8 percent, despite a 16.7 percent increase in the number of sports teams.


Player numbers also moved in opposite directions. In village centers they fell by 53.4 percent, while in city centers they rose by 20.5 percent. That means the villages’ share of all players registered at youth centers slid from about 82 percent to 63 percent in 11 years.


It is not only a matter of a long-term, slow shift. Between 2023 and 2024 alone, matches at village centers fell 28.3 percent, while the number of teams rose 21.8 percent,

according

to CAPMAS’s 2024 bulletin.


During Monday’s session, Nabil

stressed

that youth centers serve as a gateway for children and young people to play sports, saying opportunities are available across all 27 governorates through 4,600 youth centers, youth development centers and camps.


The minister also made sure to mention the National Project for Talent and Olympic and Paralympic Champion run by his ministry, which he praised for producing 577 athletes who went on to join national teams across a range of sports.


Nabil presented this figure as an accomplishment. What he didn’t go over is where his ministry’s accomplishment has actually led: Egypt’s Olympic medal count was halved at Paris 2024. The largest delegation in the history of Egypt’s Olympic participation managed just three medals — a gold, a silver and a bronze — half of what Egypt took home from Tokyo 2020, where it won six: a gold, a silver and four bronzes.


And the medals fell even though the cost of preparing and sending the Egyptian delegation to Paris topped LE1 billion, up by LE777 million from what was spent on the Tokyo delegation. This brought investment per medal in Paris to more than LE333.3 million, compared with LE37.1 million per medal in Tokyo.


The National Talent and Olympic Champion Project was launched in July 2018 when President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi

met

with then-Youth and Sports Minister Ashraf Sobhy to discuss preparations for the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, following Egypt’s remarkable achievements at the Mediterranean Games.


Sobhy

described

 the project as one of the most significant national projects undertaken by the Youth and Sports Ministry to advance and develop Egyptian sports by discovering and nurturing talented generations of athletes through modern scientific methods and specialized centers tailored to the project’s sports and age groups.


According to Sobhy, this project was to be “Egypt’s future and hope” for the 2024 Olympics and the upcoming 2028 games.


For more on the project and what went on behind it, read Mada Masr’s August 2024 report, How (not) to make an Olympic champion,

here

.

Youth and sports in rural areas: Greater access or declining participation?

author: Mzi Velapi
title: ‘End hunger, stop climate harm’: protesters take demands to Parliament
content:
About 200 residents and activists marched through the streets of Cape Town on World Food Day, calling for the government to end hunger and stop climate harm. Organised by the Climate Justice Charter Movement (CJCM) and the South African Food Sovereignty Campaign and allied partners, the protesters handed the memorandum to parliament where they called for the adoption of the People’s Sovereignty Act No 1 of 2024, a People’s Sovereignty Policy and an immediate ban on pesticides.


At least 14 to 15 million people in South Africa live below the food poverty line and experience regular food insecurity, while 11,000 children die due to malnutrition every year, and 10-million tonnes of food go to waste every year, according to Unite Against Hunger.


A recent report by the International Panel of Experts on Sustainable Food Systems (IPES-Food) found that nearly 1.4-billion people in the world work in the agrifood sector, including farmworkers. Despite their number and the vital role they play, they are among the most exploited workers in the world.


Speaking to

Elitsha

, Kara Mackay from Women on Farms Project said that women farmworkers bear the brunt of lack of access to food because of the unequal power relations that govern their relationship with farm owners. “The issue of poor wages and the high prices of food is linked to unequal power relations where the farmer is seen as the producer and the farmworkers as merely consumers,” she said.


Retired farmworker, Magrieta Prins from De Doorns said that farmers deny workers the opportunity to grow their own food by controlling their access to water. “Farmworkers do not have land to grow their own food but even in instances where they are allowed to do so, the farmer controls their use of water and in most times just deny them access to water,” Prins said.


A seasonal farmer from Ceres, Charmaine Lynx said that not having access to water impacts on their ability to produce their own food. “The social grants play a crucial role during off season. I have to look after my daughter and family during off season as I share my AllPay grant with them. Some have to resort to recycling as a means to put food on the table for their families,” said Prins.


One of the demands of the protesters is the implementation of the climate emergency social contract, that requires the government and the corporations which promote and profit from fossil fuels, pay the price.


Communities on the coastal areas of the Western Cape are experiencing severe weather that has impacted on their ability to feed their families. Fisher woman from Buffels Baai in the Southern Cape, Sarah Niemand said that the weather patterns have resulted in cold waters and fish migrating away. “For the past two months we struggled to get fish because they are scarce because of the bad weather,” she said.


Addressing the protesters outside of parliament, activist and academic, Vishwas Satgar said that southern Africa is heating at twice the global average rate, pushing the region toward an estimated 3°C of warming as global mitigation targets face severe shortfalls. “We are here to tell this government that we are not going to pay the price for their failure of leadership to prepare this country. Climate signs are telling us that El Niño is coming and the last El Niño resulted in collapsed food systems and pushed the food prices up as a result,” Satgar said.


Responding to the memorandum, Mfuneko Toyana said that the government will announce additional funding to respond to El Niño, when the minister of finance tables the Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement next week.


Satgar responded to this news: “It does not add up, this is the government that is squeezing the working class and the poor in this country. They are driving austerity meaures, and this is just a modest gesture given that the problem is big and El Niño is coming.”

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister and the Terms of Freedom
content:
Something changes when a woman occupies an office men have treated as their natural inheritance. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri’s

appointment

 on 29 September 2026 makes that change visible in Morocco. For women whose competence is routinely scrutinised, the pleasure is neither naïve nor trivial.


But the woman forming a government and the woman labouring in the fields, raising children without pay and denied an equal share of her inheritance encounter power differently. Representation changes who governs; emancipation changes what all women have the power to do. That distinction shifts our attention from PM Mansouri’s gender to the politics of the centre-right

 Party of Authenticity and Modernity (PAM

)

, which she leads. Will its programme redistribute the resources and rights on which women’s freedom depends?


The history beneath the headline


Calling women’s leadership foreign to Morocco requires forgetting its history. Historian Osire Glacier

documents

 women’s authority long before the contemporary premiership. Kenza al Awrabiya, the Amazigh mother of Idris II, helped secure the Idrisid dynasty, founded in the late eighth century in what is now Morocco. Zaynab al Nafzawiyya influenced eleventh-century Almoravid politics around Aghmat, near Marrakech. Sayyida al Hurra governed Tétouan, a city in northern Morocco, during the sixteenth century. Khnata bint Bakkar intervened in eighteenth-century dynastic politics.


Across the region,

Dihya

 is remembered as an Amazigh queen who led resistance to the Arab conquest in the Aurès, in present-day Algeria, during the late seventh century. Tuareg oral tradition remembers

Tin Hinan

 as a queen and founding ancestress of noble lineages in the Ahaggar, in present-day southern Algeria.


These histories expose how male authority is made to appear natural. Fatima Mernissi’s

The Forgotten Queens of Islam


challenges that selective memory. Colonialism also reorganised authority: French Protectorate administrators

reshaped

 customary courts around imperial priorities. What survives as tradition can carry the history of political intervention. 


Religious interpretation can give exclusion another claim to permanence. Islamist and other conservative opponents invoke this

hadith

 against women’s political authority:


«لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً»


Usually translated as saying that a people governed by a woman will not prosper, it becomes a prohibition irrespective of her competence. Asma Lamrabet, a

Moroccan Islamic feminist thinker

, questions turning a

narration linked

 to Persia’s dynastic succession into a universal ban. She reads it against the Qur’anic Queen of Sheba, whose judgement demonstrates capable leadership. Her argument contests male authority’s claim to divine necessity.


PAM’s promises and its record


Women have long contested how authority is distributed within the family. Fatima Sadiqi

documents

the Union de l’Action Féminine’s 1992 million-signature campaign to reform the Moudawana, Morocco’s family code. The 2004 reform abolished wives’ duty of obedience but retained unequal inheritance and exceptions to the marriage age of eighteen. Proposals announced in December 2024 left fundamental equality demands unresolved. In October 2025, more than sixty civil society organisations and public figures

joined to call for comprehensive reform

. Rights in Morocco have advanced through organised demands, not the gender of an officeholder.


PAM, a centre-right party founded in 2008,

advocates

 social modernisation and positions itself against the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD). It entered government in 2021 alongside the National Rally of Independents and conservative nationalist Istiqlal. Opposition to Islamist conservatism, however, does not itself entail reforming the laws and economic conditions that subordinate women.


PAM’s

2026 programme

 promises improved widow pensions, childcare, safe transport, a women’s enterprise fund and labour inspection. The commitments leave inheritance equality, abortion reform and decriminalisation of consensual same sex relations unaddressed. Mansouri called for

banning child marriage

 without exceptions in 2024, yet PAM’s electoral programme

omits that commitment

. Employment can support independence, but a wage does not cancel criminalisation or unequal property rights. The programme leaves those constraints intact.


Even PAM’s narrow promise to increase …

author: WoMin
title: Press Release | Women’s Climate Assembly strengthens Pan African solidarity, women-led resistance and the struggle for a just future
content:
“

Empowering women is a radical way to transform the world!

” –

Ivorian activist


The fourth regional

Women’s Climate Assembly

 (WCA), held in Yaoundé, Cameroon, from 5–8 October 2026, concluded with a powerful reaffirmation of African women’s determination to defend their lands, territories, livelihoods and communities, and to demand climate justice and reparations.


Under the theme, “

Our lands, our voices: African women united for climate justice and reparations!

”, the Assembly convened over 75 women community leaders, activists, feminist organisations, civil society groups and allies from twelve countries including Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Guinea-Conakry, Liberia, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Senegal and Zambia.


The gathering provided a vital space for women on the frontlines of the climate crisis, extractive industries, land dispossession and environmental destruction to share their experiences, strengthen relationships across borders and build collective strategies for change.


As the Assembly closed, one message rang clear: African women are not merely bearing the costs of the climate crisis. They are leading the struggle for solutions, defending their communities and shaping the future they want.


“

There’s an adage in my village that women cannot build a nation. The Women’s Climate Assembly has proved that women build nations. We counter this adage with the unity and solidarity of African women!”

 –

DRC activist-participant


Turning shared struggles into collective power


From communities confronting oil and gas expansion and destructive mining to women defending forests, seeds, water sources and ancestral lands, participants brought forward the lived realities of communities too often excluded from decisions about their territories and futures.


Through collective reflection, popular education and movement-building, women connected struggles that may take place in different countries but are rooted in common systems of exploitation, inequality and environmental destruction.


Designed by women activists and members of the WCA Steering Committee, the thematic teach-ins explored a range of political concepts, questions and practices, including:


The erosion of farmers’ seeds

: A challenge for building resilient and sustainable food systems. What solutions are there for preserving our seed heritage?  


Nature Commons

: The defence of the Congo Basin’s forests.


Counting the Costs of Mal/Bad Development and Demanding reparations

: The case of the African Development Bank campaign.


Fighting some of the false solutions to the climate crisis

: Gas extraction, enclosure of our forests and lands for carbon trading, green conservation and more.


Building democratic, accountable, ‘loving’ leadership

: Why are these principles so important to feminist leadership? What else do we feel is critical to leading as feminists?


Lessons on organising and movement building

: Growing National/sub-regional grassroots movements.


Building knowledge from what we know

: Building feminist popular knowledge as the basis for Building Women’s Power. How can we go about doing this locally in our communities and beyond that.


The WCA celebrated the knowledge, resistance and organising power of rural, Indigenous, peasant and working-class women. The

Each One, Teach One

 sessions embodied this spirit of knowledge-sharing, collective learning and liberation. On Day Two, participants exchanged practical skills, crafts and tools, sharing techniques for making baobab candies, producing eco-briquettes from cassava and creating seed bricks to cultivate and protect Indigenous seeds. Weaving, cloth-dyeing, beadwork and other practices also featured, affirming the value of knowledge held, practised and passed down through generations of women.


The gathering reaffirmed the importance of strengthening a Pan African ecofeminist movement that recognises the connections between the climate crisis, extractivism, gender injustice, food insecurity and the loss of community control over natural resources.


It also reinforced a fundamental principle: communities must have the power to determine their own futures, including the right to say NO to destructive development projects that threaten their lands, livelihoods and ways of life.


Climate justice means reparations, not empty promises

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: Dennis Ward
title: ITK president hopes we’ve learned from the past as the world’s interests turn to Inuit Nunangat
content:
While Natan Obed says this will be his last term as president of

Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami

 (ITK), he says there is still a lot of unfinished business and big things on the horizon.


As an example, Obed, who is into his 11th year leading the ITK, the national organization representing Inuit interests in Canada, says “it seems like the world’s interests are descending upon our homeland.”


“Strategically, Inuit Nunangat is at the forefront of global considerations,” says Obed, referring to the traditional and contemporary homeland of Inuit in Canada.


“The defense and security of this country and the territorial integrity of this country is at stake,” says Obed on the latest episode of Face to Face.


The federal government has announced more over $30 billion in funding for military and defense in Inuit Nunangat. The investments would go towards airfields, hangars and other facilities in Yellowknife and Inuvik, N.W.T.,  Iqaluit, Nunavut and Goose Bay, Labrador.


Operational hubs and bases have also been announced for Resolute, Cambridge Bay and Rankin Inlet in Nunavut.


For Obed, the interest in Inuit Nunangat is reminiscent of what happened during the Second World War and Cold War.


“Over the next 15 to 20 years, then there were installations that were built all across the Canadian Arctic and that forever transformed the lives of Canadian Inuit,” says Obed.


“We were insulated by colonization in many ways because of the Canadian government’s inability to be authoritative over our lives, but that infrastructure that was built allowed for the government of Canada to then go in and demand that our children go to residential schools, that we be coerced into communities, that we be placed in different locations to uphold Canadian sovereignty.


“So, the infrastructure that was built during that World War 2, Cold War era, allowed for the Canadian government to take away our self-determination,” adds Obed.


Obed says Inuit do not begrudge Canada for investments in protecting its territorial integrity and meeting its NATO targets. However, Obed says when there is an opportunity to support Inuit society and spend on defense, those need to be explored.


Obed would also like to “elevate” the partnerships with CSIS the department of defense to better understand the threat level.


“Foreign actors, those who wish to do nefarious things within our homeland, are going to try to destabilize our politics; they’re going to try to build and push unrest within our populations.


“So, the delivery of essential services and doing things like trying to eliminate tuberculosis with us, those are types of things that build solidarity and build this connection that Inuit have with this country and push back what is certainly coming which is other nefarious actors trying to use our socio-economic status as a wedge between Inuit and Canada as a nation state,” says Obed.


Obed, seen here announcing the location for Inuit Nunangat University, is lobbying Ottawa to help with dozens of major projects. Photo: Mark Blackburn/APTN.


ITK has its own list of 79 major projects, representing $31 billion over the next ten years that it would like to see undertaken.


In the wake of the federal government’s Bill C-5, that was narrowed down to 17 essential infrastructure projects, including hydro and natural gas lines, and aviation infrastructure upgrades.


Some of those projects would allow for the opening up of resource development.


Another major project Obed would like to see construction on before his final term is up is the long-planned

Inuit Nunangat University.


The hope is to have Canada’s first Inuit led, public Arctic University up and running in Arviat in 2030.


It is the biggest project that ITK has ever done, outside of support work for land claim agreements.


Obed is hopeful the federal government will adopt enabling legislation so they can achieve degree granting status.


He believes the university would be transformative for students.


“You can imagine going to a university, within Inuit society, within an Inuit community, to not have to leave your homeland to do that,” says Obed. “We’re also going to do this ourselves, we’re not partnering with a southern based institution for our degree granting status, we are doing this from the ground up, we are creating a governance model.


“We have already gone down the road of creating a trust, we have over $160-million in pledged funds and we are now talking with the municipality …

author: Mike Ludwig
title: Lawyers Accuse Trump of Building a “Deportation Assembly Line” for Children
content:
A new lawsuit argues that Trump administration policies are robbing migrant children of due process.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The Trump administration has stripped protections from unaccompanied migrant children and undocumented minors to fast-track deportations, a new lawsuit challenging the administration argues. The administration’s policies have created harrowing scenes in courts across the country, where an increasing number of kids appear before judges without a lawyer or the legal support necessary to navigate a complex legal system that will determine their future.

One legal organization that is part of the suit described representing a child with a documented heart condition who applied for asylum based on her experiences of sexual abuse in her home country. She was forced into a hours-long virtual asylum interview one day after being hospitalized for a cardiac event. She requested to end the interview because she was experiencing pain in her chest, visibly crying and clutching her heart. The asylum officer insisted she continue; only after hours of subjecting this child to severe distress did the officer agree to reschedule.

In the lawsuit, filed in a federal court in Maryland on October 15, a coalition of immigration advocates and legal aid providers say the administration has ignored federal law to create a “deportation assembly line” for unaccompanied children and undocumented minors.

The number of unaccompanied minors removed from the U.S. has more than tripled compared to President Trump’s first term, according to ProPublica. Children who have parents or sponsors in the U.S. have been separated from them and denied due process within Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) byzantine system of detention centers and jails, the lawsuit argues.

In some cases, children who crossed the border to seek asylum and, in many cases, to be reunited with family in the United States, could potentially be deported back to the dangerous conditions they attempted to flee, according to Cristel Martinez, an immigration attorney in Chicago.

“It’s basically sending the kids back to countries where their life is in danger, and may end up getting killed,” Martizen told reporters on October 15.

Martinez is herself an immigrant, and her law office has represented more than 400 unaccompanied minors in immigration court. That job has become increasingly difficult under a series of policy changes made by the Trump administration to fast-track deportations and cut off federal funding for nonprofits that provide legal support established by Congress for unaccompanied children. Attorneys previously had months to gather documents, perform psychological evaluations, and prepare a case. Now judges are setting asylum hearings and issuing removal orders at a speed never seen before.

Mickey Donovan-Kaloust, a director of children’s representation at the Immigrant Defenders Law Center, a plaintiff in the lawsuit, said she has worked with undocumented children for 15 years but has never witnessed the “chaos, cruelty, and disregard for due process that I’m seeing today.”

“The government is stopping at nothing to fast-track the deportations of these children,” Donovan-Kaloust told reporters on Friday. “Instead of promptly releasing children to their family members as the law requires, the government has been trapping children in government custody for months on end.”

Minimum standards for caring for unaccompanied migrant children were not established until the Flores Settlement of 1997, a consent decree resulting from years of litigation filed by human rights groups. Then, until the early 2000s, children who arrived at a U.S. border without a parent or guardian were often detained indefinitely in a prison system designed for adults and could not meet basic childhood needs such as education.

Pushing for a bill to reform these practices in 2008, Sen. Dianne Feinstein described witnessing a 15-year-old girl appear “shackled and in prison clothing” at an asylum hearing ostensibly about her seeking safety in the U.S.

“As she told her story to an immigration judge, she could not wipe away her tears because her hands were chained to her waist,” Feinstein said at the time.
