content:
Author

: SA

Title

: On Political Ecosystems

Date

: August 5 2026

Source

: Retrieved on 2026-10-21 from

<organisemagazine.org.uk/2026/08/05/on-political-ecosystems>


 We recently had a few members of National Rebirth in Preston. They popped up with a table and some of their fascy literature and ugly flags, and attempted some conversations with passers by. They were spotted by members of our local antifascist ecosystem, who took photos, shared information in community group chats, and observed.


 I wasn’t there at the time. Being a more militant organism in our local ecosystem, I would have happily gone down and told them to get the fuck back to whatever rock they crawled out from under and never return. We had a brief chat in one of our groups and opinions on National Rebirth are mixed: some consider them to not be much of a threat, or not a serious threat, but I am not so sure.


 I took a look at their website and was particularly surprised to find some very transparent writings about their aims, strategies, and branch goings-on. All veiled with the usual fascist dogwhistles and indirections of course. There is one article in particular I found very interesting, and which I want to deconstruct here.


 In “The Nationalist Ecosystem – It DOES exist, and it is a curse, not a blessing”, Grand Wizard Alek Yerbury develops an analysis of the disconnects between ‘nationalist’ activists and local communities. To briefly summarise Yerbury’s argument, he views “protests, demonstrations and street movements” and “‘Auditing’, ‘Youtubing’, and ‘Streaming’” as “staple activities of this nationalist ecosystem” which is ultimately doing nothing but perpetuating itself, and will “never develop into real political power”. Having recently read D. Hunter’s “Chav Solidarity”, I was surprised to find some parallels with his analyses, of the disconnects between “capital heavy” activists and people who are poor, working class, or criminalised. Hunter makes similar observations of the anarchist and leftist ecosystems from the other side, as a member of a local community trying to participate in what is in effect somebody else’s political ecosystem. He talks about escaping from a violent and racist upbringing, only to find countless activists and activist groups unable to engage with him or people like him with anything but contempt. As he puts so eloquently:


 I believe that the working class in this country has been thoroughly stratified, in a way which makes revolutionary change almost impossible, but I believe this can be repaired. It requires those who sit at the top of the pile to understand that they are living off bread crumbs, and in many cases I think they do, but what isn’t recognized enough is that when they catch bread crumbs, others are going without. And for sure, we should want the whole fucking loaf, but people are gonna find it hard to fight for that loaf if they’re hungry and it’s gonna be even harder if they’re being told what to do by people who are keeping the crumbs they catch to themselves.


 Both Yerbury and Hunter point to the ways political activists of all stripes cut themselves off from the very people outside of their movements that they want and need to bring into their movements. For Yerbury, the “parallel society” constituted by the far right’s organising activities are a distraction, “an echo chamber of pre-vetted, pre-screened people”. His point is that the internal cultures we develop through our collective practices might bring us closer together, but are also inherently exclusionary, forming shibboleths, and presenting barriers to audiences and potential new members, who must learn our language, so to speak. For Hunter, radical leftist spaces may preset themselves as inclusive, while also completely lacking all the individual and collective interpersonal and structural skills that are needed to actually include people who are different from us. Further, he shows how this situation is a deliberate construction of white supremacy, cisheteropatriarchy, capitalism, and the class system:


 If I was unable to pay my rent or feed myself in a socially acceptable fashion, or sub-culturally acceptable by squatting and skipping, would I be treated in comradely fashion? Perhaps. But if I lived with the stress of going day to day without knowing where my next meal would come from or where I would sleep, would I behave in ways that would be acceptable? If I was still being told I was worthless, would I …

title: Am autoritären Kipppunkt: „Law and Order“-Politik hat Konjunktur
content:
Dossier


„… In der Klimaforschung ist ein Kipppunkt ein Moment, an dem – laut Weltklimarat – „eine kritische Grenze“ erreicht wird, „jenseits derer sich ein System umorganisiert“, neue Prozesse sich verfestigen und negative Dynamiken sich beschleunigen. Dies lässt sich auch auf gesellschaftliche Kipppunkte übertragen. Kipppunkte entstehen nicht zufällig, sie sind das Ergebnis länger zurückliegender destruktiver Prozesse. Doch im Gegensatz zum Klima sind gesellschaftliche Prozesse nie unumkehrbar. Allerdings sind etablierte Diskurse, Strukturen und Normen oft nicht rückgängig zu machen. Sind autoritäre Kipppunkte überschritten, wird der Boden brüchig, auf dem plurale und demokratische Gesellschaften stehen…“

Kommentar von Daniel Mullis, Maximilian Pichl und Vanessa E. Thompson vom 16. Juni 2023 in der taz online


, siehe mehr daraus und dazu:


[„Der Widerspruch gegen Rechtsextremismus erscheint dem Staat als Skandal“] Die Würde des Rechtsextremisten


„Die Frage des SPIEGEL, ob Deutschland nach links zu rutschen drohe, wirkt in einem Land, das seit Jahren jede Debatte durch die Linse eines angeblich allgegenwärtigen linken Feindes betrachtet, inzwischen wie ein Stück Realsatire. Während Politiker, Leitartikler und Talkshowrunden sich gebetsmühlenartig daran abarbeiten, dass die eigentliche Gefahr links stehe, hat sich eine bemerkenswerte Rechtsblindheit, ja Rechtsselbstverständlichkeit in Köpfen und Handlungen breitgemacht. Man zelebriert politisch wie medial jede Mücke am linken Horizont, aber übersieht den rechtsextremen Elefanten, der längst durch den fragilen Porzellanladen der Demokratie poltert. In meinem Ideal von Deutschland hätte der Staat jene jungen Menschen, die da in Halle entschlossen vor dem Tor der Synagoge standen geehrt. Er hätte ihnen aus tiefster Haltung heraus gedankt, weil sie uns vor einem beschämenden Eklat bewahrt haben. Dem Eklat, dass sich ein bekannter Rechtsextremist am Tatort eines rechtsextremistischen Anschlags auf jüdisches Leben am Tag des Gedenkens an diesen hagestolz ebendort in Szene setzt. (…)


In meiner Realität geschieht jedoch das Gegenteil. Und das auf allen Ebenen. Halle ist hier keine Ausnahme und daher auch kein Warnzeichen, sondern mittlerweile bundesrepublikanische Normalität. (…)


Eine Normalität, in welcher nicht die Würde der Opfer schützenswert erscheint, sondern die Würde dessen, der sich an ihrem Gedenktag in den Mittelpunkt drängte. Die Würde desjenigen als schützenswerter erachtet wurde, der das Gedenken an die Opfer medial wie faktisch durch seine Vereinahmung des Ortes und des Gedenkens zum Sieg über diese ummünzen wollte. Es geht hier nicht mehr um den Schutz von Würde, sondern um deren Pervertierung: Nicht dieser Affront steht hier staatlicherseits unter Verdacht, sondern der Widerstand gegen ihn. Und genau darin liegt das Bittere unserer Zeit: Der Widerspruch gegen Rechtsextremismus erscheint dem Staat als Skandal. (…)


Nicht, die gedachte Selbstverständlichkeit, dass einige junge Menschen einen Rechtsextremisten zurückgewiesen haben, sondern dass zu viele an den Wahlurnen finden, dass Rechtsextremisten wieder die Geschicke des Landes leiten sollen. Dass in den letzten Dekaden zu viele in Landes- und Bundespolitik das Verlieren des gesamtgesellschaftlichen Kompasses als Politik selbst begriffen, sich dem Rechtsrutsch nicht nur dienstbar machten, sondern diesen seit Jahren mit Macht betreiben. Da stehen wir nun. In Halle, in Deutschland. Alerta!“

title: Francs-Tireurs Partisans (1991-1999) : s'attaquer à l'extrême droite, autrement qu'avec des mots
content:
Premier article d'une série de 3 par

La Horde

 sur le groupe antifasciste marseillais des Francs-Tireurs Partisans


Nous avons décidé de revenir sur certains événements marquants de l'histoire de l'antifascisme hexagonal contemporain, pour remettre en lumière une histoire militante parfois méconnue dans nos propres rangs et éclairer les luttes d'aujourd'hui avec les combats d'hier. Voici le premier des trois épisodes d'une petite histoire du groupe marseillais Francs-Tireurs Partisans qui, dans la dernière décennie du

XX

e

 siècle, s'en est pris aux intérêts du Front national dans la région de Marseille.


Première partie (1/3) : Les Francs-Tireurs Partisans, genèse d'un combat antifasciste à Marseille.


Marseille, 7h le matin du 15 octobre 1999. Au terme de huit années d'enquête la police arrête à leurs domiciles Yves Peirat et William Ferrari. Ces deux militants libertaires sont accusés d'avoir commis des attentats sous le nom de «

 

FTP

 

» pour Francs-Tireurs Partisans, un acronyme qui convoque l'imaginaire de la résistance à la dictature de Vichy et à l'occupant nazi. Le groupe marseillais qui se réclame de l'antifascisme radical a mis en action une forme de «

 

résistance active

 

». Il a «

 

officiellement

 

»

 [

1

]

 revendiqué 12 attentats entre 1991 et 1998, en grande majorité dirigés contre les intérêts du

FN

. Des agissements qui se limitent à des destructions matérielles, les enquêteurs eux-mêmes souligneront qu'aucun engin n'était destiné à tuer. Leur histoire est la collision d'un moment et d'un environnement particulier. La région Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur est alors le terrain de conquête privilégié de l'extrême droite. Elle y trouve enfin l'occasion d'accéder aux affaires, bien aidée par l'inconsistance et parfois la complaisance d'adversaires politiques n'opposant que la vacuité de discours rendus caducs par l'affairisme et le clientélisme ambiant. Le

FN

 progresse à grands pas, emportant par exemple des mairies. Son discours prospère sur un racisme qui n'a rien de latent, hérité de la guerre d'Algérie. Revenir sur l'histoire des

FTP

 c'est se reposer la sempiternelle question de la performativité du militantisme antifasciste et révolutionnaire. Subir les offensives et les offenses de l'extrême droite : jusqu'à quel point

 

? Ou, pour le dire de manière à la fois explicite et poétique : «

 

Je ne cherche pas à changer les règles du jeu, mais le jeu lui-même.

 

»

 [

2

]

 Une phrase d'André Breton mise en exergue parmi les revendications des

FTP

. Une histoire récente qui mérite d'être remise sur l'établi parce qu'elle renvoie les militant·e·s pour l'émancipation à des dilemmes politiques et moraux dont nous ne sommes loin de nous départir.


L'extrême droite méridionale : la rage et la revanche en bandoulière


Pour comprendre l'irruption des

FTP

 dans le paysage politique il faut revenir sur une des spécificités de la région Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur : «

 

L'arrivée successive de deux communautés issues du même pays, l'Algérie, mais dont l'une portait sa rage et sa revanche en bandoulière a permis la renaissance d'une xénophobie jamais totalement éteinte depuis les chasses à l'Italien du début du siècle (

Franc-Tireur, n°1, février 2000

)

 

». Cette arrivée autour de 1962 et la guerre coloniale qui l'a précédé représente la matrice historique qui a conduit à la création du

FN

. À l'exemple de Jean-Marie Le Pen, jeune député poujadiste, qui s'engage volontairement en Algérie fin 1956 où

il participe activement à ce qui ne peut être qualifié autrement que de torture

. Parmi les différentes factions à la création du

FN

 on retrouve nombre de nostalgiques de l'Algérie française (Roger Holeindre, Pierre Sergent) dont d'anciens membres de l'

OAS

 (Organisation Armée Secrète)

à l'origine de nombreux attentats en Algérie et en France

. L'extrême droite dispose donc d'un terreau favorable en

PACA

, même si dans les années 1970 le

FN

 stagne à un niveau électoral très faible, encore disqualifié dans les urnes et la vie politique publique par sa filiation avec Vichy, la collaboration et le nazisme. La libération n'est pas si lointaine et les blessures restent vives. Cela n'empêche pas les diverses composantes de l'extrême droite d'affirmer leur présence par des actions clandestines violentes et spectaculaires.

author: Maharnav Bhuyan
title: Why the far right’s favorite target is Indians
content:
A handful of men from the far-right National Workers Alliance yelled this at a rally for Indian democracy near Victorian Parliament on October 18. They chanted “Go back, go back” and held a blue banner stating “START REMIGRATION”, the right’s euphemism for mass deportation.

Police removed an uninvited speaker and moved the group aside.

The rally, backed by The Humanism Project and Hindus for Human Rights, answered with a chant of their own: “We welcome migrants.” The protest was called to support the youth-led protests that have filled India’s streets since early October, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign because the electoral rolls dropped more than 130 million names.

The Indian Express revealed in September that two of Kumar’s fellow commissioners had objected at least 14 times in 10 months, including to decisions allegedly made without their knowledge. The commission insists its revision decisions were unanimous.

Kumar was appointed under a 2023 law that removed the Chief Justice from the selection panel and handed the government two of its three seats. In April, the presiding officers of India's parliament refused to admit opposition notices, signed by 193 MPs, to remove him.

One placard in read: “They deleted my name, not my voice.”

Nativism is the idea that a nation belongs only to its “native” people. One Nation and India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) speak it fluently.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson told the National Press Club in June that Australia should be a “monocultural society”. Prime Minister Narendra Modi told a 2024 campaign rally that the opposition would hand people’s wealth to “infiltrators”, remarks widely condemned as an attack on Muslims. Hanson has twice worn a burqa prop into the Senate and was suspended last November for seven sitting days.

Both parties offer an anxious majority “civilisational” pride and an “enemy” within.

The anthropologist Arjun Appadurai named the engine beneath both, in 2006, as an “anxiety of incompleteness”, in which a majority turns on a small minority because it reminds it that its dream of a pure nation is unfinished.

Hindutva (the BJP’s Hindu nationalism) and Hansonism rise in different mountains and meet in the same muddy confluence. I call this mirror nativism: one grammar, two peoples, each able to see the other only as a threat.

That is why Australia’s far right has never warmed to Modi.

Before he addressed more than 20,000 people at Marvel Stadium on July 9, the far-right March for Australia promoted an anti-migration protest. Outside the stadium, a small far-right contingent protested Indian immigration and Modi himself.

Nearby, the Alliance Against Islamophobia protested his record on Muslims. One protest opposed what Modi does and the other opposed what he is.

It is often assumed that the far right hates Indians because there are so many of us.

The numbers say otherwise. The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) in June last year counted 971,020 India-born residents — 3.5% of the population — and, for the first time on record, the largest overseas-born group.

Second came the English-born at 970,950. Seventy people separate the two communities. Nobody marches against the English!

The far-right’s favourite statistic fares no better. March for Australia flyers claimed: “More Indians in 5 years, than Greeks and Italians in 100”. AAP FactCheck found that net migration from Greece and Italy over the century was 517,883, almost double India’s largest-ever five-year figure of 279,450.

India supplied 48,326 of the 185,001 permanent migration places in 2024-25 and more new citizens than any other nationality over 2023-2024.

About 110,000 Indian students, or 16% of all international students, studied here in the first half of this yea. It is roughly one India-born resident in nine. We pay full fees and a $2000 visa charge. We keep university budgets afloat. We are told our rooms are why rents go up.

We cannot vote. But those who are citizens can, which is what alarms Liberal Senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price, who told the ABC last year that “there is a concern with the Indian community”, citing its numbers and its Labor vote. She was removed from the opposition frontbench.

In Truganina, in Melbourne’s west, more than a quarter of residents were Indian-born at the 2021 Census.

Hated as transients and hated as voters makes us the convenient stranger. Sociologist Georg Simmel, in 1908, defined the stranger as one …

author: winter oak
title: When is a “fascist” not a fascist?
content:
by Paul Cudenec, who reads the article

here


Troy Southgate (1965-)

 is someone whose name I have been hearing, on and off, for thirty-odd years now, particularly at the time when my political path crossed with that of the late Richard Hunt, who was being shunted out of the anarchist scene at the same time that I was wandering into it.


Southgate was one of the “far right” nationalists who took an interest in Hunt’s green anarchist philosophy – he contributed to his review

Alternative Green

 and ended up editing it.


He got in touch with me after I published my August 2026

article

 about Hunt’s thinking, [1] pointing out his friendship with the neglected thinker and suggesting that today his and my outlooks are closer than one might have imagined.


I have to admit that I have been long been put off by Southgate’s use of the term “national-anarchism” – he founded the National-Anarchist Movement in the UK.


For me the term is an oxymoron, national identities (rather than tribal or communal ones) having been manufactured to encourage emotional attachment to the “national” states – always anarchists’ enemies – which were, in fact, the first phase of the centuries-long programme of global centralisation.


But I learned from an

audio interview

 of Southgate (

pictured

) by Luke Dodson and Adam Ormes that there was a pragmatic reason behind this label – as a convert to anarchism, thanks to Hunt, he wanted to bring other nationalists along with him. It was a bridge between two different ideological positions. [2]


Although I believe that rooted and cohesive communities are the best defence against predatory centralisation, and recognise the value of kinship ties, I am a bit wary of the position on racial separatism adopted by Southgate’s group, despite the fact that it is by no means racist, purist or dogmatic.


The

National-Anarchist Manifesto


states

: “The ‘national’ component of the term National-Anarchism centres on the fact that some of us are racial separatists. Needless to say, whilst we wish to form Anarchist communities that are ethnically organic we also oppose negative and counter-productive attitudes that encourage racial hatred or mindless violence…


“The National-Anarchist Movement (N-AM) is not a racial separatist organisation

per se

 and neither do we believe that it is essential for everyone to accept this principle. We adhere to the principle of ‘live and let live’ and, if people wish to establish multi-racial communities whilst retaining the ‘National-Anarchist’ label, then they should be permitted to do so.


“In other words, we believe that supporters of both mono-racialism and mixed tribal communities can work together for the wider promulgation of National-Anarchism in general. The most important thing of all, however, is for each of our communities to be established with a unifying vision; be it racial, cultural or spiritual. Separatism for some, mixed tribes for others”. [3]


I would suggest that if the “national” component refers to racial separatism and yet you do not have to be a racial separatist to be a national-anarchist, then perhaps the name is not a good fit for the ideology!


Moreover, if the idea is simply for people to be free to gather in communities with a certain unifying affinity, under the supposition that ethnic identity might be that affinity for some, why even bother to

name

 “racial separatism” as a possibility? Why not just leave it at the “live and let live” principle and allow human nature to take its course when the time comes for people to seek out their tribe?


The notion that folk should be free to form a community

with whomsoever they wish

 (

including

 on an ethnic basis) is already embraced by anarchism as a whole – by authentic anarchism, in any case – so that awkward “national-” prefix could then safely be ditched!


Southgate seems to have been picked out as a particular bogeyman by the system and has a

profile

 on

Wikipedia

 in which we are told that “he has been affiliated with far-right and fascist groups, such as National Front and International Third Position…


“In 1998, Southgate and other ENM [English Nationalist Movement] members founded the National Revolutionary Faction. In 2001, Southgate and the NRF were the subject of a

Sunday Telegraph

 article, in which the NRF was accused of being a neo-Nazi organisation infiltrating animal rights groups to spread fascism”. [4]


But is he

really

 a “fascist” or a …

title: Franco Cavalli: The left’s weakness fuels the far right’s rise
content:
The rise of far-right and racist movements across Europe is deepening concerns about the continent's political future. The growing strength of Alternative for Germany (AfD), the increasing political influence of the far right in France and the policies of Giorgia Meloni's government in Italy have reignited debates about Europe's future. The economic crisis, the so-called “migration crisis”, growing inequalities and social discontent fuelled by neoliberal policies are among the key factors driving the rise of the far right.


What dynamics lie behind the rise of the far right in Europe? Why have left-wing movements been unable to offer a strong alternative? What is the relationship between the crisis of capitalism and fascist tendencies? We put these questions to Swiss politician and physician Franco Cavalli. Cavalli spoke to ANF about developments in Europe, drawing particular attention to the dangers posed by Germany's rearmament policies and the rise of the AfD. He said the left had largely embraced neoliberal policies over the past three decades, arguing that the rise of the far right was driven not only by the economic crisis but also by the ideological and political weakness of the left.


How do you assess the rise of the far right in Europe? Is it possible to describe what we are witnessing today as the threat of a new form of fascism?


Both yes and no. I think we need to be careful about calling too many things fascism, because some of them may not correspond exactly to the real fascism we knew a century ago. However, it is also clear that there are many similarities between what is happening today and what happened a hundred years ago.


The situation may vary somewhat from country to country. However, if we define fascism as an ideology based on racism, one that gives absolute priority to the national population and seeks to establish an authoritarian state, then we have to acknowledge that there are many similarities, at least in terms of its fundamental principles.


We have seen this in Italy, for example. Meloni used genuinely fascist rhetoric when she was still only the leader of her party. Now that she is in government, she has considerably softened her language. Beyond that, however, particularly when we look at Germany, Spain and, to some extent, France, we have to recognise that there are strong tendencies in Europe that closely resemble the fascism of the past. These tendencies are also present in France, despite the existence of a very strong popular movement on the left.


A heavily armed Germany frightens me more than Russia


What frightens me most, of course, is Germany. Germany has decided to invest enormous sums in its military and has declared that it wants to have the most powerful army in Europe.


Therefore, if the AfD comes to power tomorrow and takes control of a Germany with a very powerful army, that would naturally be extremely dangerous. It would be far more dangerous than what is currently described as the Russian threat.


I am much more afraid of a Germany armed to the teeth than of Russia, which is actually quite weak today and has no interest whatsoever in attacking the West.


Fascism emerges from the middle class with the support of big capital


As for the reasons behind this, I think we are essentially dealing with the consequences of an economic crisis that has hit the middle class particularly hard. We know that fascism almost always emerges from the middle class with the support of big capital.


Today, the middle class is experiencing a crisis as it becomes increasingly proletarianised, and it refuses to accept this situation.


The European left, on the other hand, has weakened considerably over the past thirty years, since the collapse of the Soviet Union. It no longer has a model to rely on. It has also largely internalised neoliberal counter-reforms.


As a result, the left has moved towards the centre. In fact, something similar happened to a certain extent a hundred years ago. When the left can no longer respond to the problems of the proletariat or the increasingly proletarianised middle class, these people turn to the far right. The far right then offers proposals that appear to be solutions but are not solutions at all.


I therefore believe that the two main factors explaining the rise of the far right in Europe are the economic crisis and the weakness of the left. When these two factors come together, the far right grows stronger.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Nobel Peace Laureate Navi Pillay Calls US’s ICC Sanctions “Totally Unacceptable”
content:
Pillay led the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

We speak with the acclaimed South African human rights lawyer and international jurist Navi Pillay, who was awarded this year’s Nobel Peace Prize. Pillay has been the United Nations high commissioner for human rights and a judge at both the International Criminal Court and at an international tribunal investigating the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. Most recently, she led the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry that concluded Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Hours after Pillay was announced as winner of the Nobel Prize, the United States imposed sweeping new sanctions against the International Criminal Court.

“It’s extremely shocking to me, totally unacceptable, that the United States administration can today impose sanctions against the International Criminal Court,” says Pillay, speaking to Democracy Now! from The Hague.

Navi Pillay is now 85 years old. She was born into an Indian Tamil family in apartheid South Africa in 1941. The first woman to start a law practice in Natal, South Africa, in 1967, Pillay began her legal career defending anti-apartheid activists including Nelson Mandela, exposing torture, and helping establish key rights for prisoners on Robben Island. Mandela, as president, later appointed Pillay to the High Court of South Africa, making her the first woman of color on that bench.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: Later in the broadcast, we’re going to talk about a ballot initiative here in California, which would be, if passed, the first billionaires’ wealth tax. But first, we begin today’s show with this year’s Nobel Peace Prize winner, the South African human rights lawyer, international jurist Navi Pillay. Speaking in Oslo earlier this month, the chair of the Nobel Committee announced the award.

JØRGEN WATNE FRYDNES: This year’s laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted. The Norwegian Nobel Committee has decided to award the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

AMY GOODMAN: The Nobel Prize Committee said it chose Navi Pillay as this year’s Nobel Peace Prize winner to, quote, “issue a reminder” at a time when “judges and institutions of international law are under political attack,” unquote.

Navi Pillay has served as the United Nations high commissioner for human rights and a judge at both the International Criminal Court and at an international tribunal investigating the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. Most recently, she led the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

Navi Pillay was in Nuremberg, Germany, at an annual conference of human rights lawyers and judges when she heard the news.

NAVI PILLAY: Thank you very much. Thank you very much. If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump. … The last thing I did is the delivery of the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide.

AMY GOODMAN: Hours after Navi Pillay was announced as winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, the U.S. imposed sweeping new sanctions against the International Criminal Court that target the institution as a whole. Earlier U.S. sanctions targeted individual ICC judges and court personnel. This is U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

SECRETARY OF STATE MARCO RUBIO: President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans. And that’s why today the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us, because our message is clear: The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.

AMY GOODMAN: Soon after winning the Nobel Prize, Navi Pillay visited her former colleagues at the ICC in The Hague in a show of solidarity.

title: How will we build an understanding of democratic integration?
content:
Integration represents a transitional process for achieving peace and reconciliation. Knowing that every grain of these lands, stones, trees, and flowers belongs to us, that this is our country, we will work hard to make our country more beautiful.


As freedom fighters, we will carry out pioneering work in every sphere, from the children and mothers of this country to its nature, production, technology, and all aspects of life. Until now, we have defended our honour, will, existence, and identity with weapons in this country. Now, too, we will protect and develop everything, from its economy and ecology to its water and air.


We will bring this country to a leading position in the Middle East as well. We will raise, educate, and develop the consciousness of simple and humble people on the basis of truth and beauty. In short, we dreamed of a moral and political society. We see the practical steps towards realizing this dream and the foundations of the democratic society paradigm as very strong. This paradigm has inspired the world. If we are to build society in our country on the basis of this paradigm, we must place truth, beauty, simplicity, politics, morality, and aesthetics at the centre of our efforts.


Because we love this country. We rebelled against what was wrong, against mistakes, outdated mindsets, and hearts that had grown numb. We went up into the free mountains, fought, and struggled. At times, we fought fiercely. Why? Because we rebelled against backwardness and ugliness; we struggled to build what is beautiful, what is right, and what is moral. We learned politics and brought it into practice so that we could speak beautifully.


Love requires effort. If your spiritual world is not vast, you cannot make sacrifices or give yourself wholeheartedly. The freedom fighters gave of themselves and shared what they had; dedicating themselves to this cause, they filled every moment and every hour with hard work. We will also take the lead in the construction efforts during the integration period at this level, working with dedication and committing ourselves to our society.


We have paid a tremendous price to reach this stage. We have laid the most beautiful and unassuming daughters and sons of our country to rest in the earth. We went hungry, thirsty, and sleepless; we grew tired, yet we lived with love. Because this was the path we had chosen, and we knew why. We believed that bright days would follow these dark ones. But those days would not come on their own. Through struggle, by carving our way forward with our fingernails, we made it to where we are today.


We did not get here easily. We arrived through great acts of heroism, sacrifice, hard work, and sharing. We did not merely sweat; blood and sweat became intertwined. The flower of the tree of freedom was watered with blood and sweat; this is how it grew, matured, and bore fruit. Reaching this day has required tremendous effort.


Because we love our country, we chose the most difficult struggle and went up into the free mountains. Now we will continue the struggle in cities, towns, villages, and neighbourhoods. We received the best education in those mountains, experienced and learned the finest forms of communal life and comradeship. Now we will share these experiences with our people, our society, and all the people of our country. We will achieve this by entering a communal world of thought together.


We are entering the process of democratic integration to live and to help others live. We will take the lead in the work of peace, truth, and reconciliation committees. Rather than pursuing positions of authority, we will lead society through civilian politics.


Women will lead democratic integration. We will reorganize ourselves to build a just, equal, peaceful, and free life. As women of the mountains, our hair has turned grey, but our hearts remain childlike. We retain a nature that seeks purity, simplicity, and beauty; that asks questions with curious eyes and continues its search. Yet we do not merely ask questions; we also build our own answers. We have a fighting spirit.


As women of the mountains, we will advocate for gender equality to be placed at the centre of peace negotiations. author: Equality Now
title: The Data Behind the Action: Exploring the SADC Dashboard that tracks progress on ending child marriage in Southern Africa
content:
19th October 2026


The Data Behind the Action: Exploring the SADC Dashboard that tracks progress on ending child marriage in Southern Africa


9 min read


News and Insights


End child marriage


Africa


Photo Credit: Cozar Photography


Every girl deserves the opportunity to learn, grow, and shape her own future. Across Southern Africa, governments, parliamentarians, civil society, and local communities are working together to strengthen laws, policies, and actions to end child marriage.


A decade after the adoption of the SADC Model Law on eradicating child marriage and protecting children already in marriage, the

Southern African Development Community Parliamentary Forum

 (SADC PF) and the Technical Working Group on the Implementation of the SADC Model Law on Child Marriage launch a Dashboard on core indicators tracking progress on ending child marriage and protecting girls who are already married. The Dashboard shows where action is happening, highlights what works, and points out where more effort is needed. By bringing key information together in one place, it helps advocates, policymakers, and communities monitor progress and hold everyone accountable.


On 27 November, as we mark the very first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage, the dashboard will be one of the innovative accountability tools that will be on hand to help various players in the policy and advocacy field turn promises into real, ongoing action.


What is the dashboard and why was it created?


The SADC Dashboard is a regional platform for tracking how the

Model Law on Eradicating Child Marriage and Protecting Children Already in Marriage

 is being implemented. It also serves as a tool for accountability, knowledge sharing, and decision-making, all in one place.


The Dashboard was created to solve problems like fragmented data, unclear indicator definitions, and results that are hard to compare across countries. In the past, key information often did not reach those who needed it, making it difficult for parliamentarians, civil society, and young people to see where progress was happening or where more work was needed.


The SADC PF worked with members of the Technical Working Group, including Equality Now, Plan International, Hivos, Girls Not Brides, UNFPA, UNICEF, and CARE International Zambia to create a regional Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MERL) Framework. The Dashboard was then developed to put the MERL Framework into practice.


How does the Dashboard work?


The MERL Framework sets out key outcomes, indicators, data sources, responsibilities, and minimum standards for monitoring the Model Law. The Dashboard turns this framework into an easy-to-use digital platform.


Users can view a regional summary of progress, use filters to explore different pages and views, check information for each Member State, compare countries, and read indicator definitions and data sources.


What information does it provide?


The Dashboard brings together key indicators on child marriage and the protection of married girls across SADC Member States. It also includes indicator definitions and data sources on the same platform. This transparency lets users see what is being measured, where the numbers come from, and where data is missing.


What are the four pillars of the Model Law?


The Dashboard organises its indicators around four parts of the Model Law: prevention, protection, legal and policy frameworks, and monitoring and accountability. These cover both stopping new cases of child marriage and supporting girls who are already married.


Who can use the Dashboard?


The Dashboard is designed for a wide range of users, including parliamentarians, policymakers, program managers, researchers, civil society organisations, traditional and community leaders, and young people.


The goal is to make information about child marriage clear and useful for everyone, not just technical experts.


How can parliamentarians use it?


Parliaments are critical actors in law reform, budgeting, and oversight. The Dashboard helps MPs see how their country measures up to regional standards and to other countries. They can use it to:


Prepare for oversight questions and committee work


Inform legislation and policy formulation


Make the case for budget allocations where gaps are visible


Hold dialogue with ministries and national statistics offices on data and delivery

title: Adli kontrol değil tedavisiz infaz: Hülya Gerçek’in ev hapsi
content:
Erkek şiddeti, istismar, taciz, tecavüz… Kadına yönelik her türlü şiddet… O kadar çok bunları konuşuyoruz, erkeklik suçları o kadar çok gündemimizi işgal ediyor ki ne yazık ki kadınlarla ilgili başkaca konuları konuşmaya imkan kalmıyor. Mesela kadın mahpuslar hatta biraz daha detaylandırayım, kadın hasta mahpuslar ve hatta ev hapsindeki kadın hasta mahpuslar.


Zaman zaman tartışırız: "Ev hapsindeyken deprem olsa ev hapsindeki kişi ne yapacak?" ya da "Ev hapsindeki kişi işe gidemediği için işten çıkarılır mı?" Peki ev hapsindeki kişi ağır bir hastalıkla mücadele ediyorsa ne olacak?


Mesela Hülya Gerçek… Üçüncü evre meme kanseri. Bu, kanserin meme dışına çıkarak çevre dokulara, göğüs duvarına veya koltuk altındaki lenf bezlerine yayıldığı ancak uzak organlara (kemik, karaciğer vb.) metastaz yapmadığı lokal ileri evreye ulaştığını gösteriyor.


Gerçek, 4 Mayıs 2025’te "örgüte finans sağlamak" iddiasıyla gözaltına alınıyor, ardından ev hapsi ile serbest bırakılıyor. Hasta bir kadın için bu pek de serbest bırakılma sayılmaz elbette.


Bu arada “örgüte finans sağlamak” ne demek derseniz? Şöyle, Türkiye'de terörizmin finansmanının önlenmesine dair esaslar

6415 sayılı Terörizmin Finansmanının Önlenmesi Hakkında Kanun

 ve

TCK m. 220 / Terörle Mücadele Kanunu (TMK)

 kapsamında düzenleniyor. 


Yani Gerçek’in durumunda olduğu gibi cezaevindeki bir yakına par göndermek de bu suçla ilişkilendiriliyor, ya da cezaevindeki yazarlara da telif ödemesi yapmak bu suçla ilişkilendiliyor. Evet evet. Ocak 2026’da K

or Kitap

’ın yayınevi temsilcisine, tutuklu yazar ve editörler Tonguç Ok ile Necip Baysal’a telif ödemesi yaptığı gerekçesiyle konutu terk etmeme (

ev hapsi

) şeklinde adli kontrol tedbiri uygulandı.


Benzer durumda olan ağır bir hasta mahpus Hatice Yıldız da var. Yıldız, cezaevinde tutuklu bulunan öz kızına ve kızının ihtiyaçlarını karşılayabilmesi için aynı koğuşta kalan arkadaşına PTT (Devlet Posta Kurumu) üzerinden resmi kanallarla para yatırdığı için de suçlanabiliyor. 


Bu arada hem cezaevindeki Yıldız’ın hem de GErçek’in tedavileri yarım kalıyor, bakımları yapılmıyor, kimi zaman tek kalıyorlar. 


Gerçek’in durumunda ise başka bir şaşırtıcı detay daha var, kendisi ile aynı dosyada tutulu olan diğer kişiler hakkında önce adli kontroller kaldırılıyor, ardından 2 Nisan’da hepsi beraat ediyor. Buna rağmen Hülya Gerçek hakkında uygulanan ev hapsi kaldırılmıyor. Bu da insanın aklına Gerçek’e yönelik başka özel bir öfke mi va sorusunu akıllara getiriyor? Neden?


Anayasa’nın 17. maddesi yaşam hakkını ve kişinin maddi ve manevi varlığını koruma hakkını, 56. maddesi ise herkesin sağlık hizmetlerinden yararlanma hakkını güvence altına alıyor. Avrupa İnsan Hakları Sözleşmesi’nin 2. ve 3. maddeleri uyarınca devletin yaşamı koruma ve insanlık dışı ya da onur kırıcı muameleyi önleme yükümlülüğü bulunuyor.


Birleşmiş Milletler Ekonomik, Sosyal ve Kültürel Haklar Sözleşmesi’nin 12. maddesi ise herkesin ulaşılabilir en yüksek sağlık standardına sahip olma hakkını tanıyor. 


En yalın hali ile Anayasa, yasalar ve uluslararası düzenlemelere rağmen Hülya Gerçek hakkında uygulanan adli kontrol tedbirinin devam ettirilmesi; ölçülülük, gereklilik ve orantılılık ilkeleriyle bağdaşmıyor. 


DEM Parti Milletvekili Çiçek Otlu, Adalet Bakanı Akın Gürlek'in yanıtlaması talebi ile 7 Ekim'de Gerçek'le ilgli bir soru önergesi sundu.  "Aynı dosya kapsamında tutuklu bulunan şüpheliler tahliye edildi diğer şüpheliler yönünden uygulanan adli kontrol tedbirleri kaldırıldı. 2 Nisan'da görülen karar duruşmasında dosya kapsamındaki tüm sanıklar hakkında beraat kararı verildi. Buna rağmen Hülya Gerçek hakkında uygulanan ev hapsi tedbirinin sürdürülmesi, hukuki değil keyfi bir uygulama izlenimi yaratmakta, eşitlik ilkesine ve adil yargılanma hakkına aykırılık oluşturuyor" dedi. 


1412 hasta mahpus 


Geçen hafta ise bu kez HDK Eş Sözcüsü / DEM Parti Erzurum Milletvekili ve Anayasa Komisyonu Üyesi Meral Danış Beştaş, Gerçek’in durumunu Meclis gündemine taşıdı. “Ağır veya kronik hastalığı bulunan kişiler hakkında konutu terk etmeme yükümlülüğü kararı verilirken sağlık durumunun, tedavi gereksinimlerinin ve hastaneye erişim imkânlarının değerlendirilmesine ilişkin Bakanlığınızca belirlenmiş bir usul, kriter veya genelge bulunuyor mu?” diye sordu.

author: Ridah Hassan
title: Manosphere making classrooms toxic
content:
“I had male students threatening to rape the female students consistently. They would play ‘rape marry kill’ and used my own name frequently in their ‘game’.”

“Students saying ‘good girl’ to teachers.”

“Less respect for female staff vs male in behaviour—even with the same approaches they instantly listen to males more. More inappropriate jokes—racism, homophobic and sexist jokes with little consequences. Visible [and] audible dismissal/rejection of female staff to their faces when they appear to take classes.” 

These are quotes from a Monash University report which has cast light on the disturbing sexist conditions faced by teachers and students in primary and secondary schools across the country. 

Duty of Care: Teachers’ experiences of sexism, misogyny and sexual harassment in Australian schools

 is based on the testimony of 2,600 educators and reveals the breadth and depth of the crisis. 

A common theme in the report is the lack of respect male students show female teachers. This includes frequent interrupting, ignoring of instructions, mocking and mimicking, speaking disrespectfully and refusing to accept responsibility when challenged about inappropriate behaviour. Physical aggression and intimidation were also reported, along with threats of more serious physical and sexual assault. Male students frequently make “derogatory comments toward females focusing on appearance and worth”, “jokes about gender roles e.g. the kitchen”, “inappropriate sexualised remarks about female bodies, including specifically about peers and/or staff” and “[making] sexual noises in the classroom” while female staff are trying to teach.

This behaviour is contributing to the burn-out of teachers in a profession already facing shortages due to poor pay and unmanageable workloads. One respondent put it clearly: “Being the front line and bearing the brunt of misogyny is exhausting and erodes self-worth”. According to the report, 77 percent of teachers say that sexism and misogyny have a “negative” or “very negative” impact on their wellbeing, and more than 50 percent of female teachers report that they either “occasionally” or “frequently” consider leaving the profession because of it. And the situation is getting worse—both primary and secondary teachers reported that gendered violence on the part of students had increased significantly in the previous twelve months.

Given adult teachers are feeling undermined, threatened and belittled by male students’ behaviour, the impact on teenage girls should be cause for immediate action. According to the report, “Younger students are comfortable using misogynistic language without thought e.g. calling girls in class a ‘slut’ ‘whore’ because they won’t share a highlighter”, and “Women/girls in class are okay with being treated with misogyny as this is seen as ‘normal’ now. They do not retaliate and internalise, making emotional regulation hard”. Another teacher observed: “Female students are scared to speak out and express their opinions in class with males who chastise them. I am noticing students are very hesitant to participate in discussion these days whereas it used to be female students being quite eager to share ideas and answer questions. Female students appear angrier than in the past as well”.

Male students direct sexist and misogynistic language towards their female peers freely, entrenching a toxic gender divide among students. Again, the statistics bear this out, with 80 percent of respondents agreeing that the behaviour is having a negative impact on student wellbeing. In observing and being victim to male students’ sexism—including constantly disrupting learning and making spaces hostile—girls are being socialised to accept dehumanising language and treatment and to make themselves small targets by withdrawing and accommodating to the selfish and anti-social behaviour of boys. 

And though there are undoubtedly some who are willing to challenge their peers’ appalling behaviour, it is an unacceptable environment for female students to be expected to navigate every day, while at the same time trying to do the actual tasks of deciphering Shakespeare or learning calculus. It is well established that students learn best when they feel safe, supported and respected. This is currently not the case for female students at Australian schools.

author: Tam Saavedra
title: Conectivas: First Time in (Por primera vez en) CADF
content:
A table of our own: Conectivas First Time in CADF.    

 


 


For many years, we have seen organizations that serve people with disabilities occupy spaces like the Central American Donors Forum (CADF); this year, thanks to WEI’s support, we were able to attend in person, make our voices heard, and become visible in places where we are usually invisible.   

 


We were not there to hear people speak about us; we went there to speak ourselves, for the first time and in first person – as an organization led by women with disabilities.   

 


What did we achieve?

  

 


We facilitated a networking table on women and disability.  

 


We offered support to WEI’s lighting talk on women with disabilities fighting back anti rights movements.   

 


We networked with different actors about how we see – from a human rights perspective- the backlashes in rights we are seeing globally and how we want to be included in the resistance.  

 


They still see us as something apart.

  

 


Most of the donors we engaged in conversations agreed that the disability movement needs funding but struggled to see how to include us into what they are already doing.

Disability intersects with democracy, protection and gender equality.

Yes, we need specific resources and at the same time, inclusion is necessary in the actions already put in place.  

 


Our accessibility is not enough. We could get there and participate thanks to WEI’s support, but many other women are missing from the conversation.

A

rriving is not enough: we need conditions to remain and continue participating in those spaces

. To guarantee accessibility for women with disability the following spaces are also needed:   

 


Dedicated spaces for rest 

 


Physical and menstrual hygiene accommodations  

 


Spaces where we can isolate from noise and crowds 

 


To invest in the participation of the feminist disabled leaders is to invest in the movements:

it strengthens the local networks that already exist to access resources, but also to weave alliances that survive the forum’s duration.   

 


Thank you to Women Enabled International for the technical assistance they provided, it opened up space for us, instead of just occupying it.

This time we had a table of our own: what comes next is that this stops being the exception.

  

 


In solidarity,  

 


Conectivas

 · October 2026. 

 


 


Una mesa propia: Conectivas por primera vez en CADF

  

 


 


Por muchos años hemos visto cómo organizaciones que prestan servicios a personas con discapacidad ocupan espacios como el Foro Centroamericano de Donantes (CADF) y este año gracias al apoyo de WEI pudimos estar en persona, poner nuestra propia voz y hacernos visibles donde solemos ser invisibles. 

 

 


No fuimos a que hablaran de nosotras; fuimos a hablar, por primera vez y en primera persona, como organización representativa de mujeres con discapacidad 

 

 


¿Qué logramos?

 

 

 


Facilitamos una mesa de networking sobre mujeres y discapacidad  

 

 


Apoyamos la charla relámpago de WEI sobre mujeres con discapacidad frente a movimientos antiderechos. 

 

 


Conversamos con distintos actores sobre cómo vemos, desde los derechos humanos, los retrocesos que estamos viviendo, y también sobre cómo queremos incluirnos. 

 

 


Nos siguen viendo como un punto a parte.

 

 

 


La mayoría de donantes con quienes conversamos dicen que necesitarían recursos específicos para discapacidad, pero no ven cómo incluirnos en lo que ya hacen.

L

a

 discapacidad atraviesa la democracia, la protección y la igualdad

 de género. Sí, necesitamos recursos específicos y, a la vez, inclusión en las acciones que ya existen.  

 

 


Nuestra accesibilidad no es suficiente. Nosotras pudimos llegar gracias al apoyo de WEI, pero faltan muchas otras, y

llegar no basta; necesitamos condiciones para quedarnos.

Para garantizar la accesibilidad de mujeres con discapacidad también son necesarios espacios para: 

 

 


Descansar 

 

 


Higiene corporal y menstrual 

 

 


Aislamiento del ruido y de la multitud,  

 

 


Invertir en la participación de líderes feministas con discapacidad es invertir en movimientos:

fortalece las redes locales que ya existen, tanto para acceder a recursos como para tejer alianzas que duren más que el foro. 

 

 


Gracias a WEI por una asistencia técnica que nos abrió espacio sin ocupar nuestro lugar.

author: Eliel Peterson
title: Death as liberation
content:
Death as liberation is hardly a comfortable political proposition to digest. In a world where Black death is often the common condition, there is a well-established insistence on our living. So what do we make of two of Africa’s greatest filmmakers, Ousmane Sembène and Souleymane Cissé, whose earliest cinematic visions, expressed through their respective debut features

Black Girl

 (1966) and

Den Muso

 (1975), center on the suffering, alienation, and eventual deaths of Black women?

Sembène’s

Black Girl

 is preoccupied with racial violence and the economic exploitation that continues to structure relations between Senegal and France. The film follows Diouana, a young Senegalese woman who accepts employment with a white French family and travels to Antibes believing she is embarking on a new life. While Cissé’s

Den Muso

, turns inward, examining interpersonal violence and the ways patriarchal power consumes family life and communities, weakening the broader social fabric of a nation. The film follows Tenin, a mute young woman who becomes pregnant after being raped, exposing the brutal underbelly of the patriarchal violence imposed upon her. Despite the differences in their circumstances, both films position death as a troubling possibility of liberation for their central characters.

Tenin (Dounamba Dany Coulibaly) in a still from Souleymane Cissé’s

Den Muso

 (1975).

The history of Black resistance has not solely been confined to the preservation of life. From enslaved Africans who leapt from ships during the Middle Passage, to those who faced death in the fight against their oppression,

It is true

 that to rather die than to endure is not a popular or digestible form of liberation. Although these acts are not equivalent, nor do they carry the same weight as the deaths of these fictional characters, Sembène and Cissé, raise an uncomfortable question: what does life mean for a person stripped of agency, recognition, and self-determination?

For Diouana and Tenin, freedom remains out of reach because of the structures governing their everyday lives that continually deny these women full humanity: Tenin’s father and her rapist, Diouana’s white employers. This sustained stripping of humanity produces what I would argue is already a death, albeit a social one, that precedes their physical endings. Sembène and Cissé challenge audiences by asking what is living for the dehumanized. Diouana travels to France only to find her livelihood replaced by isolation and unpaid, alienated labor, while Tenin’s body becomes a site upon which familial and communal shame, punishment, and control are dumped. Death, therefore, is at the core of both films from the outset, existing not only as a shocking culminating event, but as a condition of violence. By the end of each film, Sembène and Cissé are not arguing over whether death is a worthy or noble choice for self-liberation; rather, they position the act of self-annihilation as the only remaining form of control available to their characters, and as an indictment of a society in which death is the only option. 

It is understandable to recoil at the self-inflicted violence that ultimately claims both Diouana and Tenin. One might ask why their rage is not directed solely towards those who harmed them. Why does Tenin’s retaliation extend beyond her rapist? Why doesn’t Diouana exact revenge on her employers and flee France? These questions linger because death feels like an unsatisfying conclusion, one that denies us, as audiences, the catharsis of resistance. We want these women to fight back and survive. We want their suffering to lead somewhere other than death. Yet perhaps the more daunting question is not why these women die, but whether we find their deaths more difficult to accept than the suffering that precedes them. What is ultimately more uncomfortable to confront: their deaths, or the conditions that made life itself unbearable?

Neither film offers an uncomplicated answer. To read Diouana’s and Tenin’s deaths as acts of liberation is not to suggest that their deaths resolve the violence they endure, or that self-annihilation is freedom in any complete sense. Their deaths do not dismantle the structures that dehumanized them. What death offers these women, perhaps then, is not freedom but a final assertion of agency within those systems. This is what makes their endings so devastating: the possibility of control emerges only when the possibility of living on their …

title: Imperial dominance has always been linked with sexual violence (Entertainment Labor for Palestine)
content:
A post shared by Entertainment Labor for Palestine (@entertainmentlabor4palestine)

Imperial dominance has always been linked with sexual violence. author: Erin Reed
title: Anti-Trans Ads May Be Backfiring on Republicans
content:
Elon Musk’s America PAC has committed $100 million to a midterm push heavy on anti-transgender ads.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

In the first few weeks of October, three national pollsters asked three different questions about transgender issues, and all three landed in the same place from different angles: the anti-transgender ads this year may be backfiring on Republican strategists. Navigator Research, AP-NORC and ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos polls collectively found that voters trust Democrats on transgender issues and rank those issues as not very important to their vote, and that Republican and independent voters were less likely than Democrats to prioritize them. When the polls are contrasted with the massive amount of ad spend on transgender issues, there are signs, first seen in the Virginia gubernatorial election last year, that the high concentration of ads may turn voters off and could fuel, rather than suppress, a Democratic wave election in 2026.

The first poll to come out was the Navigator Research poll. In this poll, voters were asked to list up to five top issues, giving it a stronger signal than prior polls that only required voters to list their top issue. Even when voters were asked to list five, transgender issues ranked dead last among all 20 issues on the list. And Democratic voters were the most likely group to rank transgender issues a top issue, meaning many of those who did are likely voting to protect transgender rights, not to restrict those rights. Prior polls from Gallup have found similar results, although this poll is most notable due to its top-five format.

Then, another poll came out: AP-NORC asked Americans on a per-issue basis how important each issue was to their own vote. Whereas most issues asked about were considered “one of the most important,” such as the economy and the war with Iran, only 11% of respondents named transgender issues one of the most important to their vote. Furthermore, 51% of respondents said that transgender issues were “not an important issue” at all, the only issue to score higher than the teens on that question. And as we know from prior polling, Democrats are much more likely to answer that transgender issues are important to them.

Lastly, an ABC/Post/Ipsos poll has been released that outright asks Americans which party they trust to do a better job on transgender issues. Of those asked, 38% of Americans say they trust Democrats on transgender issues when compared to 29% who say they trust Republicans, a 9-point Democratic edge. Notably, Americans trust Democrats on a whole host of issues that the survey asks about, ranging from health care to the economy. Only on crime do respondents trust Republicans more than Democrats, a poor sign for the Republican Party in the lead-up to the 2026 elections.

These results are heavily contrasted by the money being spent on anti-transgender ads. According to AdImpact data, more than $100 million has been spent since Aug. 1 on more than 200 ads that use the phrase “sex change.” Meanwhile, Elon Musk’s America PAC has committed $100 million to a midterm push heavy on anti-transgender ads aimed at Democrats. EITM has received reports of mailers in several races ranging from state legislative to congressional campaigns that such data has no way of capturing, and many political pundits have pointed out that the anti-trans ad focus seems to be a defining issue in the 2026 midterms.

Republicans are starting to sound the alarm that the anti-trans ads are not working. The American Principles Project, one of the progenitors of anti-transgender ads, has admitted that such ads “may not be sufficient” on their own this election cycle for Republicans to win the midterms. And former Texas House Speaker Dade Phelan, a Republican, said last week that the ads are just “not resonating” with Texas voters. Now, these polls confirm the fears of Republican strategists about the effectiveness of the ads.

If all of this sounds familiar to EITM readers, it is because similar dynamics played out around the same time in 2025 in Virginia’s gubernatorial and House of Delegates elections. Voters, when asked who would better handle transgender issues, named Abigail Spanberger, the Democratic candidate for governor, over Winsome Earle-Sears, the Republican. Despite this, Earle-Sears kept pouring more and more money into …

author: Unknown
title: I can’t find the source now but someone went back and studied MOGAI culture on tumblr in the 2010s…
content:
confession theres a lot of lgbt microlabels and contradictory identities and xenogenders that i 100% do not understand no matter how many explanations i see. but my logic when i encounter someone who flies those flags is “well, i doubt anyone would land on those labels without putting a whole lot of thought into their identity, so thats none of my business” . this attitude has served me well and will continue to serve me well forever i think. good luck with that you crazy kids.

I can’t find the source now but someone went back and studied MOGAI culture on tumblr in the 2010s and found that

Over 50.000 new identities and flags were coined in a few years.

Most described some state of being unsure, undefined or inbetween.

Most were used once or twice and then never again, not even by the people who coined the term and designed the flag.

While that could be seen as a negative thing, former participants generally looked back positively on these single-use microlabels as something that gave them room to explore and removed the pressure of choosing something definitive.

So the lesson here was: sometimes someone uses a microlabel because they’re not done putting thought into their identity, and that’s also a great reason to have a microlabel. Getting the ‘what am I?’ question out of the way by choosing a deliberately vague microlabel can be a way to make space to just exist, to experience queer life without the pressure of labeling it any further. That’s very useful and hella queer.

title: Ozgul Sakiyê li Metrîsê serdana girtiyên LGBTÎ+ kir: Hevgirtin wan bihêztir dike
content:
Parlementera Stenbolê ya Partiya Wekhevî û Demokrasiyê ya Gelan (DEM Partî) Ozgul Sakiyê li Girtîgeha Metîsê serdana LGBTÎ+yên girtî kir. Operasyonên navborî di 12ê Îlonê de li dijî  rêxistin, aktivîst û cihên LGBTÎ+yan hatibûn kirin. Di wan operasyonan de gelek LGBTÎ+ hatibûn girtin.


Sakiyê têkildarî serdana xwe li ser hesabê xwe yê medyaya civakî daxuyanî daye. Sakiyê diyar kir ku girtiyan ji xizm û heskiriyên xwe re slav şandin.


Li Stenbolê di operasyonên li dijî LGBTÎ+yan de 20 kes hatin girtin


17 Îlon 2026


Sakiyê da zanîn ku mehek li ser girtîbûna wan re derbas bûye û bertek nîşanî ne berdana wan da.


“Tevî ku tu sedemeke tune ye da ku rojekê tenê jî girtî bimînin, di yekem nirxandina girtîbûnê de jî nehatin berdan.”


“Piştgiriya li derve hêzê dide wan”


Sakiyê ragihand ku mercên girtîgehê li gorî rojên destpêkê baş bûne û anî ziman ku ew bi rêvebirê girtîgehê re jî civiyaye û hin daxwazên girtiyan gihandine rêveberiyê.


Sakiyê diyar kir ku LGBTÎ+yên ku wê dîtiye, bi taybetî bal kişandine ser girîngiya piştgiriya li derve:


“Her yek ji wan bi cihêyî anî ziman ku piştgiriya li derve hêzê dide wan.”


Sakiyê destnîşan kir ku divê girtî di demek nêz de serbest bên berdan û daxuyaniya xwe bi banga piştgiriyê bi dawî anî:


“Lêbelê tişta herî girîng ew e ku em ji bo ku ew di zûtirîn demê de azadiya xwe bi dest bixin, têkoşîn û piştgiriyê kêm nekin.”


Polîsan bi ser Kaos GLyê de girt: Polîs ketin komeleyê, rêveber hatin desteserkirin


14 Îlon 2026


Çi bûbû?


Di 12ê Îlonê de di çarçoveya operasyonên “Malbata min di ewlehiyê de ye” polîsan li gelek bajaran bi ser komeleyên LGBTÎ+yan, malên aktivîstan û mekânên cuda de girtin.


Di operasyonan de gelek kes hatin desteserkirin. Di heman demê de malperên înternetê yên rêxistinên LGBTÎ+yan û hesabên medyaya civakî yên aktivîstan hatin astengkirin.


Derbarê neh LGBTÎ+ yên li Stenbolê hatibûn girtin de, di yekem nirxandina girtîbûnê ya mehane de biryara berdewamiya girtîbûna wan hate dayîn.

author: Unknown
title: Sincan’dan notlar: LGBTİ+ operasyonu tutukluları ve dayanışmanın politikası
content:
Bugün Sincan Cezaevi’ndeydim. “Ailem Güvende” adı verilen operasyon kapsamında tutuklanan sekiz arkadaşımızı ziyaret ettim: Janset, Umut, Metin, Baran, Tuğba, Nedime, Burçin ve Selin.


Bazılarıyla uzun zamandır tanışıyorum. Bazılarını ise sadece isimlerinden, politik mücadelelerinden biliyorum. Eylül’ün 12-13’ündeki baskın ve gözaltı sürecinde elimden geldiğince yanlarında olmaya çalıştım. Ardından bir süre Ankara dışında olduğum için ziyaretlerine gidemedim. Bugün, tutuklanmalarından sonra ilk kez bir araya geldik.


Cezaevi ziyareti muhalefet milletvekillerinin, bilhassa bizim partinin bir rutini. Son zamanlardaki gelişmeler sanırım CHP ve Yeni Parti’nin de çok daha sık cezaevi yollarına düşmesini getirdi. Ben de üç buçuk yıllık milletvekilliğim boyunca Sincan’a özellikle çok sık gittim. Kobani duruşmalarının sürdüğü dönemde bir ayağım neredeyse hep oradaydı. O davadan tutuklanan arkadaşlarımızı, Gezi tutuklularını, farklı siyasi davalardan içeride bulunanları fırsat buldukça ziyaret etmeyi sürdürüyorum. Bakırköy, Silivri, Diyarbakır, Edirne, Erzincan, Kandıra, Sincan… Gidebildiğim cezaevleri.


Her cezaevi başka bir dünya. Gezi tutuklularının deneyimi başka, Kobani davasından tutuklananlarınki başka, LGBTİ+’larınki bambaşka. Bu dünyaları birbirine benzetmek, aralarındaki farkları silmek olur. Ama her birinde insanın özgürlüğüyle, onuruyla, bedeniyle ve hayatını kurma hakkıyla ilgili ortak bir mesele var.


Cezaevleri, dışarıdaki hayatın bir süreliğine paranteze alındığı yerler değil yalnızca. Aynı zamanda dışarıdaki eşitsizliklerin, ayrımcılıkların ve iktidar ilişkilerinin içeride başka biçimlerde yeniden üretildiği mekânlar. Üstelik kapılar kapandığında, içeride yaşananların dışarıda duyulması da giderek zorlaşıyor.


Bu nedenle siyasetçilerin, milletvekillerinin ve hak savunucularının cezaevlerini sessiz bırakmaması gerekiyor. Avukatların ve ailelerin kurduğu dayanışma elbette vazgeçilmez. Fakat dışarıdan kurulan bağların da sürmesi, içeride yaşananların gündeme taşınması, insanların yalnızca dosyalarından ibaret olmadıklarının hatırlanması gerekiyor. Siyasetçilerin bir gözünün ve bir kulağının orada olması gerekiyor. Bir ayağının orada olması gerekiyor.


Bugün sekiz kişiyle görüştüm. Sabahtan akşam mesai bitinceye dek. İçeri girerken bıraktığım Ankara, çıktığımda puslu neredeyse kar havası diyeceğim bir havaya ve yağmura teslim olmuştu. Belki de ne kadar isterlerdi o havada dışarıda olmayı, yağmurda ıslanmayı, hatta üşümeyi... Şehre bir buçuk saatte dönebildik. Sekiz ayrı hayat, sekiz ayrı hikâye. Zaman zaman güldük, zaman zaman ağır şeyler konuştuk. Her birinin kendi koşulları, kendi ruh hâli, kendi direnme biçimi var. Ama ziyaretlerin sonunda aklımda kalan, yalnızca kendilerine yapılanları anlatmaları değildi. Kendi bildik hayatları tümden ellerinden alındığında bile başkalarının hayatlarına bakmaya devam etmeleriydi.


Belki de bugün en çok bunu düşündüm.


Janset’in söylediği bir şey var. Bunları öğrenmemiz için onları ziyarete gitmemiz gerekmiyor.


Haklıydı. Hak ihlallerini, ayrımcılığı, yoksulluğu ve cezaevlerinin koşullarını öğrenmek için bunları yaşayan insanların bunu anlatmasını beklememeliyiz. Birilerinin yaşadıklarını bize anlatmak zorunda kalmadığı bir politik duyarlılık geliştirebilmeliyiz. Ne var ki çoğu zaman, bildiğimizi sandığımız şeylerin gerçek anlamını, karşımızda bir insan oturduğunda, onun hikâyesini dinlediğimizde kavrıyoruz.


İlk Janset’le görüştüm


Janset’i Ankara’daki çeşitli panellerden, toplantılardan tanıyorum. Aramızda bir dayanışma hukuku olduğunu sanıyorum. Bana bir dostum, arkadaşımmış gibi geliyor. Söylediklerinde kişisel bir sitemden çok, son derece açık bir politik itiraz vardı. Siyasetçilerin LGBTİ+’larla dayanışma konusundaki çekingenliğine dikkat çekti. Sözü dolandırmadan söyledi: Siyasetçi linci göze alacak. Cesareti yoksa da "mış gibi", dayanışıyormuş gibi yapmayacak.


Bu sözün üzerinde durmak gerek.


Siyaset, herkesin zaten rahatlıkla söyleyebildiği şeyleri tekrar etmekten ibaret değil. Başkalarının dile getirmekte zorlandığı sözleri de dile getirmek gibi bir sorumluluğunuz var. Bunun bir bedeli olabilir. Hedef gösterilebilirsiniz, linç edilebilirsiniz, hiç hak etmediğiniz saldırılara maruz kalabilirsiniz. Ama siyasetçinin meselesi, kendisini bu ihtimallerden korumak olamaz.

"Estrella: Bittersweet Freedom for a 'Bad Mexican'"

We’re joined by Latino USA host Maria Hinojosa as she shares the story of Estrella Diamantina González, an undocumented transgender woman and trafficking survivor from Mexico caught up in the United States’ criminal and immigration systems. This summer, after serving a nine-year sentence in a Texas men’s prison, Diamantina González was released, but she wasn’t free. She was immediately transferred to an immigration detention facility and then deported. Hinojosa, who has been reporting on Diamantina González’s ordeal for the last decade, followed her to Mexico in the new audio documentary “Estrella: Bittersweet Freedom for a 'Bad Mexican.'”

Maria HinojosaPulitzer Prize-winning journalist, founder of Futuro Media and host of Latino USA.

"Estrella: Bittersweet Freedom for a 'Bad Mexican'"

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman.

Soon after President Trump’s inauguration, in February of 2017, one of the first people arrested by immigration agents inside a courtroom was Estrella Diamantina González, a trans woman from Mexico. She was there to get an order of protection against an abusive boyfriend, but she never got the chance. Estrella spent most of the next decade caught up in the U.S. criminal and immigration systems. This summer, after serving a nine-year sentence in a Texas men’s prison, Estrella was deported to Mexico.

Journalist Maria Hinojosa was the first journalist to interview her after that courtroom arrest, and she’s been speaking to her ever since, for about a decade. Maria Hinojosa is the Pulitzer Prize-winning host of Latino USA. A new audio documentary is out today about Estrella, her life, her deportation and the evolving relationship with Maria. It’s called Estrella: Bittersweet Freedom for a “Bad Mexican.” This is a clip from a video that accompanies the documentary. It begins with Estrella stepping out of a bus and seeing Maria Hinojosa, who is waiting for her in Mexico City.

title: "Creemos en la potencia política de los feminismos para sembrar semillas de esperanza"
content:
Por Mariángeles Guerrero


Desde Córdoba


De todas las provincias, del campo y de la ciudad, llegan mujeres, lesbianas, travestis, trans. Viajan hace 40 años para encontrarse. Para compartir con otras lo que viven cotidianamente en sus territorios, para aprender de otras experiencias, para contar las propias. Este año, el

39° Encuentro Plurinacional de Mujeres, Lesbianas, Travestis, Trans, Bisexuales, Intersexuales y No Binaries

 se realizó el fin de semana pasado en Córdoba capital. Los temas a debatir se organizaron por ejes. En el Eje Soberanía, la soberanía alimentaria tuvo su propio taller. Carina Vallejo, de la Unión de Trabajadoras y Trabajadores de la Tierra (UTT) de Santiago del Estero rescata “la fuerza de poner en común nuestras realidades y darte cuenta de que no estás sola”.


Y añade: ”Poder encontrarnos, escucharnos y ver que las problemáticas del agua, la tierra y el modelo de producción nos atraviesan a todas por igual en distintos puntos del país nos fortalece muchísimo. Nos permite

salir del aislamiento del interior

 y llevar nuestras voces comunitarias a debates colectivos y asambleas de mujeres”.


Dhanna Moyano es travesti, productora caprina en Luján de Cuyo (Mendoza), integrante del Movimiento Nacional Campesino Indígena-Somos Tierra (MNCI-ST) y representante de Argentina en la Coordinadora Latinoamericana de Organizaciones del Campo (CLOC) - Vía Campesina. Fue una de las participantes del Encuentro y señala que la masividad que tuvo es una muestra del enojo que hay hacia el Gobierno. “

Hemos tenido travesticidios, femicidios, ventas de nuestras tierras

. Hoy estamos defendiendo la soberanía alimentaria porque es preocupante para nuestros cuerpos y cuerpas en todo el país. Este 15 de octubre tenemos que salir a defender que no nos vendan las tierras, porque venderlas es despojar a las familias campesinas, a las comunidades indígenas y al colectivo de la diversidad que está retomando ese camino”, denuncia.


Y agrega: “Nos abrazamos, lloramos, porque estamos mal en todo el país pero también estamos dando una gran lucha por un país soberano, libre y con igualdad de derechos para todos y para todas”.


Subraya que las diversidades sexuales son parte de la lucha campesina porque es un proyecto de vida concreto para ellas. “El Estado dice que las travestis nos morimos entre los 35 y 40 años por la calidad de vida que llevamos. Volver al campo implica que esa calidad de vida aumenta, porque es una vida más sana, más saludable”, explica.


Ante el desmantelamiento de las políticas para la agricultura familiar y las políticas de género,

la presencia de la realidad campesina en los debates feministas se vuelve urgente

. En este Encuentro, por primera vez la UTT, el MNCI-ST y el Movimiento Nacional Campesino Indígena marcharon en una misma columna, representando a las organizaciones campesinas.


Carolina Llorens, del MNCI-ST y del Movimiento Campesino de Córdoba (MCC) remarca “la potencia política que tenemos los feminismos de articular luchas ante un horizonte tan fragmentado y sembrar semillas de esperanza y de organización”. Y apunta que ese es el rol que tienen los feminismos campesinos, indígenas y populares. Y que los encuentros son un espacio potenciador de esa presencia política, del protagonismo de las mujeres y las diversidades.


Graciela Salto vive a 60 kilómetros de la localidad de Quimilí (departamento Moreno, al este de Santiago del Estero). Es la primera vez que participa de un Encuentro. “Aquí se dice la verdad, uno no viene con invento, dice lo que conoce. En la vida del campo es muy importante la tierra. Y si la defendemos, es para algo bueno, para algo sano. Es para la familia, para nuestros abuelos, para nuestros hijos”, valora.


Salto participó del Encuentro con la bandera del MNCI en la espalda, junto a su hija y otras compañeras que viajaron con ella. Cuenta que el mensaje que fue a compartir con compañeras de otras provincias es lo que sucede en su territorio: las fumigaciones con agrotóxicos y los desalojos. “No podemos criar animales porque te los envenenan, no podemos poner una fruta o una verdura por el tema del veneno. Y si nos desalojan, ¿adónde vamos a ir? No queremos irnos, somos nacidos y criados en el campo”.


Al encuentro llevó su bandera y la realidad del lugar donde vive. Y vuelve a su casa, dice, “con muchos recuerdos de todo lo que se habló y de las compañeras que conocí”.
